Package io.mavlink4j.codec

Class SigningClock

java.lang.Object
io.mavlink4j.codec.SigningClock
public final class SigningClock extends Object
The MAVLink 2 signing timestamp for one remote system (VERIFIED, mavlink.io message-signing spec): a 48-bit counter in 10 microsecond ticks since SIGNING_EPOCH, not Unix epoch -- a naive millisecond- or microsecond-since-1970 implementation produces a value that looks plausible and fails every verification silently (QA item 3).

The spec's own persistence rule, implemented exactly

"[The timestamp] should be monotonically increasing... incremented... at least once every time a message is sent... stored in persistent storage, ideally at least once a minute; the timestamp used on startup should be the maximum of the timestamp implied by the system clock and the stored timestamp." This class is that rule and nothing else: loadPersisted/ persist are plain functional collaborators (the library has no storage of its own; the host supplies one), so a backward-jumped local clock (a VM snapshot restore, an NTP step) can never regress the sequence below what was last durably saved (QA item 1) -- next()'s first call seeds from max(system, stored), never system alone.

One instance is scoped to one remote system id (see SigningClocks), shared between the outbound-signing use (FrameWriter calling next() for every frame addressed to that vehicle) and the inbound-verification use (SignatureVerifier calling observe(long) after accepting a signed frame from it) -- the spec's own "keep systems synchronised" rule, applied per remote system rather than process-wide.

Two meanings, two fields

current() is this side's own outbound sequence -- monotonic across a restart because it is seeded max(system, stored), wall clock included. floor() is the inbound freshness reference SignatureVerifier checks a vehicle's frames against: the highest timestamp this side has accepted from, or handed to, this vehicle, seeded from loadPersisted alone -- never the wall clock. A vehicle with no real-time clock (pymavlink, or an ArduPilot before its GPS/GCS sets one) can only advance its own clock from frames this side sends it, so measuring it against a wall-clock-seeded value after a restart longer than the stale tolerance would reject it forever; measuring it against the floor lets a resumed vehicle keep sending at the pace it already proved it could reach.

Thread-safe via a single monitor; called at most once per outbound/inbound frame, never a contention hot path.

    • current

      public long current()
      The last value handed out by next() or observed via observe(long). Never increments.

    • floor

      public long floor()
      The highest signature timestamp this side has accepted from, or handed to, this remote system -- see the class-level "Two meanings, two fields" note. Seeded from loadPersisted only (so a never-heard vehicle floors at 0, not this process's boot time); raised only by observe(long), never by next().

    • observe

      public void observe(long remote)
      Folds a remote timestamp into this clock: both current() and floor() become max(existing, remote). Never moves either backwards -- the spec's own "keep systems synchronised" rule, applied after accepting a signed frame from this remote system, or after handing one a timestamp via SETUP_SIGNING (see SignatureVerifier and MavlinkSigningPushService respectively).
